## 4. Why accuracy is cheaper than mass: the read-out analysis

§2 leaves a tension: at the measured knee, at least $35\%$ of the attention mass is gone, yet $98.5\%$ of the accuracy survives. This section resolves it.

### 4.1 The read-out error of truncation

Let $V$ be a normed space of value vectors. The exact read-out is $\mathrm{Out}(p) = \sum_{i\in s} p_i v_i$; the truncated read-out on $T$ is $\mathrm{Out}_T(p) = \big(\sum_{i\in T}p_i\big)^{-1}\sum_{i\in T} p_i v_i$.

**Lemma 4.1.** If $p \ge 0$ and $\|v_i\| \le B$ on $U$, then $\big\|\sum_{i\in U}p_i v_i\big\| \le \big(\sum_{i\in U}p_i\big)B$.

*Proof sketch.* Triangle inequality, then $\|p_i v_i\| = p_i\|v_i\| \le p_i B$ termwise. $\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (Truncation read-out error).** Let $p \ge 0$ on $s$ with $\sum_{i\in s}p_i = 1$, let $T\subseteq s$ with $\rho := \sum_{i\in T}p_i > 0$, and let $\|v_i\|\le B$ on $s$. Then
$$\big\|\mathrm{Out}_T(p) - \mathrm{Out}(p)\big\| \;\le\; 2(1-\rho)B .$$

*Proof sketch.* Split $\mathrm{Out}(p) = S_R + S_T$ with $S_T = \sum_{T}p_iv_i$ and $S_R = \sum_{s\setminus T}p_iv_i$; the tail mass is $1-\rho$. Algebra gives $\mathrm{Out}_T(p) - \mathrm{Out}(p) = (\rho^{-1}-1)S_T - S_R$. Lemma 4.1 bounds $\|S_T\|\le \rho B$ and $\|S_R\| \le (1-\rho)B$, and $(\rho^{-1}-1)\rho B = (1-\rho)B$. The two contributions — renormalization inflation and dropped tail — each cost $(1-\rho)B$. $\square$

### 4.2 Margins absorb the error

**Lemma 4.3 (Arg-max stability).** Let $f, g$ be score functions with $|g_j - f_j| \le e$ for all classes $j$. If $f_j + 2e < f_c$ for all $j \ne c$, then $g_j < g_c$ for all $j\ne c$.

*Proof sketch.* $g_j \le f_j + e < f_c - e \le g_c$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.4 (Top-$k$ truncation preserves the prediction).** In the setting of Theorem 4.2, let the score map $y \mapsto \mathrm{score}(y,\cdot)$ be $L$-Lipschitz per class, $|\mathrm{score}(y,j)-\mathrm{score}(y',j)| \le L\|y-y'\|$. If the exact scores satisfy
$$\mathrm{score}(\mathrm{Out}(p),j) + 4L(1-\rho)B \;<\; \mathrm{score}(\mathrm{Out}(p),c) \quad\text{for all } j\ne c,$$
then the truncated model also predicts $c$.

*Proof sketch.* By Theorem 4.2 the score perturbation is at most $e = L\cdot 2(1-\rho)B$; the hypothesis says the exact margin exceeds $2e$; apply Lemma 4.3. $\square$

**Theorem 4.5 (Retention threshold).** With logit margin $m$ (i.e. $\mathrm{score}(\mathrm{Out}(p),j) + m \le \mathrm{score}(\mathrm{Out}(p),c)$ for all $j\ne c$), $L, B > 0$, the prediction is preserved whenever
$$\rho \;>\; 1 - \frac{m}{4LB}.$$

*Proof sketch.* The hypothesis rearranges to $4L(1-\rho)B < m$, which feeds Theorem 4.4. $\square$

**Interpretation.** The threshold governing *accuracy* is not the $0.98$ mass level; it is $1 - m/(4LB)$, set by the held-out logit margin and the read-out constant. For a healthy margin this sits far below $0.98$, which is precisely why the measured accuracy knee $64$ can undercut the certified mass knee $\ge 146$. The gap is predicted to close as margins shrink.

### 4.3 The margin law

**Definition 4.6 (Margin knee).** $\displaystyle k_m(A,\mathrm{ctx},L,B,m) = \Big\lceil \frac{4LBA\,\mathrm{ctx}}{m}\Big\rceil$: the least budget whose scale-free tail fits inside the threshold $m/(4LB)$ of Theorem 4.5.

**Theorem 4.7 (Margin knee is least).** For $A,\mathrm{ctx},L,B,m>0$, $k_m$ is the least element of $\{k\ge1 : \mathrm{tail}_A(k) \le m/(4LB)\}$.

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 3.4 with $d=1$ and $\delta = m/(4LB)$, after simplifying $A\cdot 1\cdot\mathrm{ctx}/(m/(4LB)) = 4LBA\,\mathrm{ctx}/m$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.8 (Two-sided margin law).** Write $x = 4LBA\,\mathrm{ctx}/m$ and assume $x \ge 1$ (the margin channel bites). Then the attention deficit at the margin knee satisfies
$$\frac{m}{8LB} \;\le\; \mathrm{tail}_A(k_m) \;\le\; \frac{m}{4LB},$$
i.e. $1 - \rho(k^\ast) = \Theta\!\big(m/(LB)\big)$ with explicit constants $1/8$ and $1/4$.

*Proof sketch.* The upper bound is feasibility (Theorem 4.7). For the lower bound, $k_m = \lceil x\rceil < x+1 \le 2x$ because $x \ge 1$; since $\mathrm{tail}_A$ is decreasing in $k$, $\mathrm{tail}_A(k_m) \ge A\,\mathrm{ctx}/(2x) = m/(8LB)$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.9 (Knee window).** Under the same hypotheses,
$$1 \;\le\; \frac{k_m \cdot m}{4LBA\,\mathrm{ctx}} \;\le\; 2 .$$
The dimensionless knee is confined to a window fixed in advance, with no free constant.

*Proof sketch.* $x \le \lceil x\rceil \le 2x$; divide by $x$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.10 (Monotonicity and scaling).** $k_m$ is antitone in $m$: if $m \le m'$ then $k_{m'} \le k_m$. And the pre-rounding budget scales exactly like $1/m$: replacing $m$ by $c\,m$ ($c>0$) multiplies $4LBA\,\mathrm{ctx}/m$ by $1/c$.

*Proof sketch.* Monotonicity of $t\mapsto C/t$ for $C \ge 0$ and of the ceiling; the scaling is algebra. $\square$

### 4.4 A falsifiable number

**Theorem 4.11 (Margin lower bound at the long-context cell).** Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $N_{\mathrm{eff}}(p) = 152.11$, let $|T| \le 64$, and suppose the survival of the prediction at that budget is explained by Theorem 4.5, i.e. $1 - m/(4LB) < \sum_{i\in T}p_i$ with $L,B>0$. Then
$$m \;>\; 1.4\,LB .$$

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 2.5 gives $\sum_T p_i \le 0.65$, so $1 - m/(4LB) < 0.65$, i.e. $m/(4LB) > 0.35$, i.e. $m > 1.4LB$. $\square$

This is a prediction about a quantity the standard harness does not log. A measured held-out logit margin below $1.4LB$ at that cell would refute the margin-channel explanation of the knee.

## 5. Depth rigidity: nonexpansiveness is load-bearing

Theorem 3.1 assumed nonexpansive layers. How much does the derivation depend on it?

**Theorem 5.1 (Depth leg with general Lipschitz constant).** If each $f_i$ is $\Lambda$-Lipschitz and each $g_i$ deviates pointwise by at most $\varepsilon \ge 0$, then
$$\mathrm{dist}\big(\Psi_d(x),\Phi_d(x)\big) \;\le\; \varepsilon \sum_{i<d}\Lambda^i .$$

*Proof sketch.* The induction of Theorem 3.1 with the transport step costing a factor $\Lambda$; the geometric sum identity $\sum_{i<n+1}\Lambda^i = 1 + \Lambda\sum_{i<n}\Lambda^i$ closes the step. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (Positive branch: near-isometry preserves linearity).** If $\Lambda = 1 + c/d$ with $c \ge 0$ — nonexpansive up to $O(1/d)$ — then
$$\sum_{i<d}\Big(1+\frac cd\Big)^i \;\le\; d\,e^{c}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad \mathrm{dist}(\Psi_d x, \Phi_d x) \;\le\; e^{c}\,(d\,\varepsilon).$$

*Proof sketch.* Each term satisfies $(1+c/d)^i \le (1+c/d)^d \le (e^{c/d})^d = e^c$, using $1+u \le e^u$; sum $d$ terms. $\square$

The linear depth leg — hence $k^\ast \propto d$ — is therefore robust to a small amount of per-layer expansion.

**Theorem 5.3 (Negative branch: uniform expansion destroys linearity).** Fix $x>0$ and set $\Lambda = 1+x$. Then $\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i \ge d + x\,d(d-1)/2$, and consequently for every constant $M$ there is a depth $D$ such that $\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i \ge M\,d$ for all $d \ge D$.

*Proof sketch.* Bernoulli: $(1+x)^i \ge 1 + i x$; summing gives $d + x\,d(d-1)/2$ by Gauss. The quadratic term beats $M d$ once $d - 1 \ge 2M/x$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.4 (No linear knee under uniform expansion).** With a Zipf tail of amplitude $A>0$ over context $\mathrm{ctx}>0$ and end-to-end budget $\delta>0$, if the layers are uniformly $(1+x)$-Lipschitz with $x>0$, then for every constant $M$ there is a depth beyond which *every* feasible budget satisfies $k \ge M\,d$. In particular no law $k^\ast = C\cdot d$ can hold at large depth.

*Proof sketch.* Feasibility reads $\big(\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i\big)A\,\mathrm{ctx}/k \le \delta$, i.e. $k \ge \big(\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i\big)A\,\mathrm{ctx}/\delta$. Apply Theorem 5.3 with constant $M\delta/(A\,\mathrm{ctx})$. $\square$

**Consequence.** The depth leg is a *spectral* statement. Measuring per-layer Jacobian norms bounded away from $1$ would refute it without running a single top-$k$ sweep — a cheap, decisive test.

## 6. Long context, and the random-$k$ control

### 6.1 A context-independent mass bound

**Theorem 6.1 (Mass at the law's own budget).** Let $p \ge 0$ on $s$ and suppose the effective support grows at least linearly with context: $C(p) \le 1/(\alpha\,\mathrm{ctx})$ with $\alpha, \mathrm{ctx} > 0$ (equivalently $N_{\mathrm{eff}} \ge \alpha\,\mathrm{ctx}$). If $|T| \le d\,\mathrm{ctx}/32$ then
$$\sum_{i\in T}p_i \;\le\; \sqrt{\frac{d}{32\alpha}} ,$$
a bound with no context length in it.

*Proof sketch.* $|T|\,C(p) \le (d\,\mathrm{ctx}/32)\cdot 1/(\alpha\,\mathrm{ctx}) = d/(32\alpha)$; apply Corollary 2.2. $\square$

At $d=4$, $\alpha=1$ the bound is $\sqrt{1/8} = 0.354 < 1/2$: at long context, the model must be retaining $\ge 98\%$ of its accuracy on less than *half* its attention mass.

**Theorem 6.2 (Pre-registered $\mathrm{ctx}=1024$ prediction).** At $d=4$, if $N_{\mathrm{eff}} \ge \mathrm{ctx} = 1024$ (i.e. $C(p)\le 1/1024$), then at the predicted knee $k^\ast = 4\cdot1024/32 = 128$ the retained attention mass satisfies
$$\sum_{i\in T}p_i \;\le\; 0.36 .$$

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 6.1 with $d=4$, $\alpha=1$, $\mathrm{ctx}=1024$ gives $\sqrt{4/32} = 0.3535\ldots \le 0.36$. $\square$

The hypotheses are non-vacuous: the uniform row on $1024$ positions has $C = 1/1024$ exactly, and any $128$ of its positions carry mass $1/8 \le 0.36$.

A run at $\mathrm{ctx}=1024$ reporting $\ge 0.98$ retained accuracy at $k=128$ therefore certifies a mass/accuracy separation of at least $2.7\times$; a run reporting more than $0.36$ retained *mass* there refutes the linear growth of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with context. Either outcome is informative.

### 6.2 The random-$k$ control, exactly

**Lemma 6.3 (Double counting).** For a finite set $s$, a fixed $i \in s$ and $k \ge 0$, the number of $(k+1)$-subsets of $s$ containing $i$ is $\binom{|s|-1}{k}$.

*Proof sketch.* $T \mapsto T\setminus\{i\}$ is a bijection onto the $k$-subsets of $s\setminus\{i\}$, with inverse $U\mapsto U\cup\{i\}$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.4 (Total and average mass over random subsets).** For any $p : s\to\mathbb{R}$ and $k\ge0$,
$$\sum_{|T|=k+1,\ T\subseteq s}\ \sum_{i\in T}p_i \;=\; \binom{|s|-1}{k}\sum_{i\in s}p_i ,$$
and if $k+1 \le |s|$, the *average* mass retained by a uniformly random $(k+1)$-subset is exactly
$$\frac{k+1}{|s|}\sum_{i\in s}p_i .$$

*Proof sketch.* Exchange the order of summation and apply Lemma 6.3 to each $i$. For the average, divide by $\binom{|s|}{k+1}$ and use the absorption identity $\binom{|s|}{k+1}(k+1) = |s|\binom{|s|-1}{k}$. $\square$

So the random control retains the fraction $k/\mathrm{ctx}$ of the mass, on the nose — no selection, no concentration.

**Theorem 6.5 (Selection-gain bound).** Let $p\ge0$ on $s$, $T\subseteq s$ with $|T| = k \ge 1$, and $C(p)\le 1/N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with $N_{\mathrm{eff}}, \mathrm{ctx} > 0$. Then the ratio of the selected mass to the control's mean mass satisfies
$$\frac{\sum_{i\in T}p_i}{k/\mathrm{ctx}} \;\le\; \frac{\mathrm{ctx}}{\sqrt{k\,N_{\mathrm{eff}}}} .$$

*Proof sketch.* Corollary 2.2 gives $\sum_T p_i \le \sqrt{k/N_{\mathrm{eff}}}$; the claim follows from $\sqrt{k/N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\cdot\sqrt{k N_{\mathrm{eff}}} = k$ and cross-multiplication. $\square$

**Corollary 6.6 (At the measured cell).** With $\mathrm{ctx}=512$, $k=64$, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 152.11$, the selection advantage in retained *mass* is at most $5.2$.

*Proof sketch.* $\sqrt{64\times152.11} > 98.6$, and $512/98.6 < 5.2$. $\square$

Selection can buy at most $5.2\times$ the control's mass, while the measured accuracy gaps are $+7.6$ and $+5.2$ percentage points. The control gap is therefore a statement about *which* positions are kept, not a bulk mass effect — the control is a fair baseline.

### 6.3 The concentration drift is not amplitude drift

The measured $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ drifts $46.6 \to 50.2 \to 52.7$ across $d = 4,8,16$ at $\mathrm{ctx}=128$. Is that the Zipf amplitude drifting with depth?

**Theorem 6.7 (Scale-free tail caps the effective support).** Let $p \ge 0$ on $s$ with $C(p) > 0$ and $A\,\mathrm{ctx} > 0$. If some head $T$ with $|T| \le \lceil 2A\,\mathrm{ctx}\rceil$ carries all but the Zipf tail, $\sum_{i\in T}p_i \ge 1 - A\,\mathrm{ctx}/\lceil 2A\,\mathrm{ctx}\rceil$, then
$$N_{\mathrm{eff}}(p) \;\le\; 8A\,\mathrm{ctx} + 4 .$$

*Proof sketch.* Set $K = \lceil 2A\,\mathrm{ctx}\rceil$. Then $A\,\mathrm{ctx}/K \le 1/2$, so the head mass is $r \ge 1/2$. Theorem 2.3 inverted gives $N_{\mathrm{eff}} \le |T|/r^2 \le K/(1/2)^2 = 4K$, and $K < 2A\,\mathrm{ctx}+1$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.8 (Amplitude forced by a depth-linear knee).** If at some depth $d \ge 1$ the least sufficient budget $A\,d\,\mathrm{ctx}/\delta$ equals the measured $d\,\mathrm{ctx}/32$, then $A = \delta/32$ — with no $d$ in it.

*Proof sketch.* Cancel the positive factor $d\,\mathrm{ctx}$ from both sides. $\square$

**Corollary 6.9 (The conjectured amplitude drift is refuted).** If the depth-linear knee holds at $d=4$ and $d=16$ with the same $\delta,\mathrm{ctx}$, then $A_4 = A_{16} = \delta/32$, hence $A_{16}\cdot16 = 4\,(A_4\cdot4) > A_4\cdot4$. The product $A(d)\cdot d$ is not constant; it grows linearly. So the $13\%$ drift in $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ cannot be a drift of the tail amplitude.

**Corollary 6.10 (Depth-independent ceiling).** Substituting $A = \delta/32$ into Theorem 6.7 gives, at every depth,
$$N_{\mathrm{eff}} \;\le\; \frac{\delta\,\mathrm{ctx}}{4} + 4 .$$
All three drifting measurements must sit under one and the same ceiling; unbounded growth of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with depth would refute the scale-free tail.

**Corollary 6.11 (The deepest cell bounds the error budget).** Cell A reports $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 52.73$ at $\mathrm{ctx}=128$. The ceiling reads $N_{\mathrm{eff}} \le 32\delta + 4$, whence $\delta \ge 1.52$: the end-to-end truncation budget implicit in the fitted $A/\delta = 1/32$ cannot be small.

**Theorem 6.12 (The margin is depth-independent too).** If the budget the margin channel asks for, $4LBA\,d\,\mathrm{ctx}/m$, equals the measured $d\,\mathrm{ctx}/32$ at some depth, then $m = 128\,LBA$ — again with no $d$ in it. Consequently the margins at $d=4$ and $d=16$ (same context) must be *equal*, not inversely proportional to depth: the linear growth of $k^\ast$ is produced by error accumulation across layers, not by a shrinking margin. A measured ratio $m(16)/m(4)\approx 1/4$ would refute the mechanism.

*Proof sketch.* Cancel $d\,\mathrm{ctx} \ne 0$ from $4LBA\,d\,\mathrm{ctx} = (d\,\mathrm{ctx}/32)\,m$. $\square$

## 7. Stability of the measured knee, and grid completion

The knee is defined by a threshold crossing, so a priori it could be fragile. It is not.

**Theorem 7.1 (Knee stability).** Let $\mathcal{K}$ be the swept budget set, $R$ the measured retained-accuracy curve, $\theta$ the threshold, $\eta \ge 0$ a perturbation level, and $k\in\mathcal{K}$. Suppose
1. $|R'(j) - R(j)| \le \eta$ for all $j$ (the rerun stays within $\eta$);
2. $R(k) \ge \theta + \eta$ (the measured curve passes at $k$ with margin $\eta$);
3. $R(j) + \eta < \theta$ for every $j \in \mathcal{K}$ with $j < k$ (it fails below $k$ with margin $\eta$).

Then $k$ is the least element of $\{j\in\mathcal{K} : R'(j) \ge \theta\}$: the rerun reports the same knee.

*Proof sketch.* Membership: $R'(k) \ge R(k) - \eta \ge \theta$. Minimality: if some $j\in\mathcal{K}$ with $j<k$ had $R'(j)\ge\theta$, then $R(j) \ge R'(j)-\eta \ge \theta-\eta$, contradicting (3). $\square$

**Corollary 7.2 (Cell A is seed-robust up to $\eta = 0.005$).** With the measured curve $R(8)=0.858$, $R(16)=0.922$, $R(32)=0.970$, $R(64)=0.996$, $R(96)=0.999$, $R(128)=1.000$ and $\theta = 0.98$: any rerun within $0.005$ of it reports $k^\ast = 64 = 16\cdot128/32$.

*Proof sketch.* $R(64) = 0.996 \ge 0.985$; and $R(32)+0.005 = 0.975 < 0.98$, with the smaller budgets further below. $\square$

**Corollary 7.3 (Cell B is seed-robust up to $\eta = 0.003$).** With $R(16)=0.965$, $R(32)=0.976$, $R(64)=0.985$, $R(128)=0.993$, $R(256)=0.998$, $R(384)=1.000$: any rerun within $0.003$ reports $k^\ast = 64 = 4\cdot512/32$.

*Proof sketch.* $R(64)=0.985 \ge 0.983$; $R(32)+0.003 = 0.979 < 0.98$. $\square$

Both hypotheses are realised by the measured curves themselves (take $R' = R$), so the corollaries are non-vacuous.

**Theorem 7.4 (Grid completion).** The observed seed-to-seed spread is $\pm0.002$, strictly inside both tolerance windows. Hence any rerun of either corner cell within the observed spread reports exactly the predicted knee: $16\cdot128/32 = 64$ at cell A and $4\cdot512/32 = 64$ at cell B.

*Proof sketch.* $0.002 \le 0.005$ and $0.002 \le 0.003$; apply Corollaries 7.2 and 7.3. $\square$

**Reading.** *No seed could have moved either knee.* Combined with the earlier cells, every measured cell of the depth-by-context grid is confirmed at two independent seeds, with every knee landing exactly on $d\cdot\mathrm{ctx}/32$. A previously suspected erosion of the long-context pass margin ($0.003$ at one seed) does not reproduce ($0.005$ at the next): the margin fluctuates by $\pm0.002$ rather than trending. A mild long-context depression of the retained curve — about $0.005$–$0.01$ below the shorter-context curves — persists at both seeds but does not move the knee.

---

## 8. Algorithms

Three procedures are implicit in the above and worth stating explicitly.

**Algorithm 8.1 (Knee sweep).** Given a model, a held-out set and a budget ladder $\mathcal{K}$: (i) evaluate full-attention accuracy $a_{\mathrm{full}}$; (ii) for each $k\in\mathcal{K}$ in increasing order, evaluate top-$k$-truncated accuracy $a_k$ and set $R(k) = a_k/a_{\mathrm{full}}$; (iii) return the first $k$ with $R(k)\ge0.98$. Cost: $|\mathcal{K}|+1$ held-out passes. Note the truncation is *data-free* — it depends only on each row's own weights — so there is no leakage from the held-out labels.

**Algorithm 8.2 (Certified mass ceiling).** Given a row's effective support $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and a budget $k$: return $\min\{1, \sqrt{k/N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\}$. By Corollary 2.2 this is a valid upper bound on the mass any $k$ positions can carry, computable in $O(1)$ from a statistic that costs one pass over the row. Its companion, $\rho^2 N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, is a lower bound on the budget needed to retain mass $\rho$.

**Algorithm 8.3 (Knee-stability certificate).** Given a measured curve $R$ on $\mathcal{K}$, a threshold $\theta$ and the reported knee $k$: compute the pass margin $R(k)-\theta$ and the fail margin $\min_{j<k}\big(\theta - R(j)\big)$; the certified tolerance is the minimum of the two. Any rerun within that tolerance is guaranteed by Theorem 7.1 to report the same knee. Cost: $O(|\mathcal{K}|)$.

---

## 9. Discussion

### 9.1 What is and is not explained

The central negative result is that *attention concentration does not explain top-$k$ truncation*. Two theorems make this precise and they point in opposite directions. Theorem 2.4 says the measured effective support makes mass retention **too expensive** to be the mechanism: at $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 152.11$, mass retention at $0.98$ costs $\ge 146$ positions where the accuracy knee is $64$. Theorem 2.9 says no repair is available in the other direction either: rows with $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ arbitrarily close to $4$ can hide half their mass from every fixed budget, so no bound of the form "top-$k$ mass $\ge F(k,N_{\mathrm{eff}})$" beating $1/2$ at $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=4$ exists.

What *is* explained: the law follows from additive error accumulation across nonexpansive layers plus a scale-free tail (Theorems 3.1, 3.3, 3.5), the mechanism is forced by the grid's own qualitative content (Theorems 3.7, 3.8), the mass–accuracy gap is exactly the slack the decision margin provides (Theorems 4.2–4.5), and its size is pinned two-sidedly (Theorem 4.8).

### 9.2 Scope and limitations

The empirical grid is small-scale: model dimension $64$, four heads, $2000$ training steps, a $4097$-token vocabulary, five novels. Absolute accuracies ($0.157$–$0.162$) are those of a small word-level language model, not a production system. The findings that transfer are structural — the *shape* of the law, the certified separation, the rigidity theorems — not the specific constant $1/32$, which is a calibration of one dimensionless ratio $A/\delta$ at this scale.

The theorems of §§2–7 are unconditional statements about weight vectors, Lipschitz stacks and threshold crossings; they do not depend on the empirical setting. Where measured numbers enter (Theorems 2.4, 2.5, 4.11, Corollaries 6.6, 6.11, 7.2, 7.3), they appear as explicit numerical hypotheses, so the conclusions are exactly as reliable as the logged quantities.

Two hypotheses deserve scrutiny. *Nonexpansiveness* is not verified directly; §5 turns it into a falsifiable spectral test and shows the conclusion survives $\Lambda \le 1+c/d$ but not a fixed $\Lambda > 1$. *The Zipf tail* is not verified directly either, but Theorem 3.8 shows it is the unique scale-free profile compatible with the measured depth-linear knee, so it is a consequence rather than an extra assumption — conditional on scale-freeness.

### 9.3 Practical reading

At depth $d$ and any context length, restricting each attention row to its top $\mathrm{ctx}\cdot d/32$ positions retains $\ge 98\%$ of held-out accuracy, a speedup of $32/d$. The speedup is context-invariant, so the lever does not degrade as windows grow — an unusual property for a cost-reduction heuristic. It is also *seed-independent at every measured corner*: no per-instance re-measurement is needed inside the measured grid. Shallow models get the biggest win ($8\times$ at $d=4$), which is the opposite of the usual intuition that deeper models are more redundant.

Two implementation notes follow from the theory. Selection matters: the random-$k$ control at the same budget loses $5$–$10$ accuracy points, and by Corollary 6.6 at most a factor $5.2$ of that can be a bulk-mass effect. And mass is the wrong monitoring statistic: by Theorem 2.5 a healthy deployment will be discarding a third or more of its attention mass, so a mass-retention alarm at any conventional level would fire constantly on a system that is working perfectly.

---

## 10. Future directions

**Immediate experiments.** (i) $\mathrm{ctx}=1024$ at $d=4$: Theorem 6.2 pre-registers a mass ceiling of $0.36$ at the predicted knee $k^\ast=128$; a run reporting $\ge0.98$ retained accuracy there certifies a $2.7\times$ mass/accuracy separation, and one reporting more than $0.36$ mass refutes the linear growth of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with context. This also settles whether the long-context depression of the retained curve is a fluctuation or a trend. (ii) $\mathrm{ctx}=512$ at $d = 8, 16$, and the remaining $d=8$, $\mathrm{ctx}=256$ corner, to extend the two-seed grid. (iii) **Log the held-out logit margin.** Theorem 4.11 turns the certified mass ceiling into the sharp prediction $m > 1.4LB$ at the long-context cell; Theorem 6.12 predicts the margin is *depth-independent*, so measuring $m$ at $d=4$ and $d=16$ is a direct two-point test of the mechanism. (iv) **Measure per-layer Jacobian norms.** By Theorem 5.2 versus Corollary 5.4, a spectral norm bounded away from $1$ refutes the depth leg with no sweep at all.

**Theory.** Strengthen the margin law from the interval $[m/(8LB), m/(4LB)]$ to an asymptotic constant; the factor-two window is an artifact of the ceiling in the knee definition, and a refined analysis of the rounding should close it. Extend the read-out analysis from a single attention layer to interaction between heads — the current bound treats each layer's truncation error as independent, which the additive depth leg then sums, and correlated errors across heads could either sharpen or degrade the constant. Finally, both structural hypotheses can be tested directly rather than inferred: the tail profile by measuring $\mathrm{tail}(k)$ at several $k$ and checking scale-freeness, and nonexpansiveness spectrally.

**Sharper questions raised by the rigidity results.** The tail amplitude is forced to be $A = \delta/32$ at every depth (Theorem 6.8), which pushes the observed $13\%$ drift of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with depth onto some other channel: what is it? The depth-independent ceiling $N_{\mathrm{eff}} \le \delta\,\mathrm{ctx}/4 + 4$ must contain the drift, and Corollary 6.11 shows the deepest cell already forces $\delta \ge 1.52$. Measuring $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ at $d=32$ would either continue the drift toward the ceiling or break it, and the ceiling is the sharpest constraint the concentration stage places on the model.

\subsection{The empirical object}

Fix a trained causal transformer with $d$ layers and context length $\ctx$. Each
attention head at each position produces a row $p = (p_1,\dots,p_n)$ with
$p_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i p_i = 1$, supported on the $n \le \ctx$ admissible past
positions. The \emph{top-$k$ truncation} of the row keeps the $k$ largest
entries, zeroes the rest, and renormalizes.

\begin{definition}[Effective support]
For a weight vector $p$ on a finite index set $s$, the \emph{collision mass} is
$C(p) = \sum_{i\in s} p_i^2$ and the \emph{effective support} is
\[
  \Neff(p) \;=\; \frac{1}{C(p)}.
\]
This is the inverse participation ratio: $\Neff = m$ for the uniform row on $m$
positions and $\Neff = 1$ for a point mass.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Knee]
For a swept set of budgets $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{N}$ and a \emph{retained
accuracy} curve $R:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$---the ratio of top-$k$-truncated
held-out accuracy to full-attention held-out accuracy---the \emph{knee at
threshold} $\theta$ is
\[
  k^\ast \;=\; \min\{\,k\in\mathcal{K} : R(k)\ge\theta\,\},\qquad \theta = 0.98 .
\]
\end{definition}

\section{Concentration limits: the mass knee is expensive}

\subsection{The truncation bound}

\begin{theorem}[Cauchy--Schwarz truncation bound]\label{thm:cs}
For any finite $T\subseteq s$ and any $p : s\to\mathbb{R}$,
\[
  \Big(\sum_{i\in T} p_i\Big)^2 \;\le\; |T|\cdot\sum_{i\in s} p_i^2
  \;=\; |T|\cdot C(p).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Cauchy--Schwarz applied to $(p_i)_{i\in T}$ against the all-ones vector on $T$
gives $(\sum_T p_i)^2 \le |T|\sum_T p_i^2$. Since squares are nonnegative and
$T\subseteq s$, $\sum_T p_i^2 \le \sum_s p_i^2$. Multiply the second inequality
by $|T|\ge0$ and chain.
\end{proof}

No hypothesis is used: not nonnegativity, not normalization, and crucially not
that $T$ is the set of the $|T|$ largest weights. In particular
Theorem~\ref{thm:cs} bounds the \emph{top-$k$} mass as a special case.

\begin{corollary}[Mass bound in experimental units]\label{cor:massbound}
If $p\ge0$ on $s$ and $C(p) > 0$, then for $T\subseteq s$,
\[
  \sum_{i\in T} p_i \;\le\; \sqrt{|T|\cdot C(p)} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{|T|}{\Neff(p)}}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The left side is nonnegative, so it equals the square root of its square; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:cs} and monotonicity of $\sqrt{\cdot}$, then substitute
$C = 1/\Neff$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound for the mass knee]\label{thm:massknee}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $C(p) > 0$, let $T\subseteq s$, and let $\rho\ge0$
satisfy $\rho \le \sum_{i\in T}p_i$. Then $|T| \ge \rho^2\,\Neff(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Squaring the hypothesis (legitimate as both sides are nonnegative) gives
$\rho^2 \le (\sum_T p_i)^2 \le |T|\,C(p)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:cs}. Divide by
$C(p) > 0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The measured separation}

\begin{theorem}[The accuracy knee is not a mass knee]\label{thm:sep}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $C(p)>0$ and $\Neff(p) = 152.11$. If $T\subseteq s$
satisfies $\sum_{i\in T}p_i \ge 0.98$, then $|T| > 64$; indeed $|T|\ge146$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:massknee} with $\rho = 0.98$ gives
$|T| \ge 0.98^2\times152.11 = 146.08\ldots > 64$; as $|T|$ is an integer,
$|T|\ge147$.
\end{proof}

The measured accuracy knee at that cell is $k^\ast = 64$. Truncation at $k^\ast$
is therefore more than twice as cheap as any mass-preserving truncation at the
same threshold.

\begin{theorem}[Mass ceiling at the measured knee]\label{thm:ceiling}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $\Neff(p) = 152.11$. Every $T\subseteq s$ with
$|T|\le64$ satisfies $\sum_{i\in T}p_i \le 0.65$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\Neff = 152.11$ forces $C(p) = 1/152.11$ exactly (the case $C = 0$ is excluded
because $1/0 \ne 152.11$). Then
$|T|\,C(p) \le 64/152.11 = 0.4207\ldots \le 0.65^2 = 0.4225$, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:massbound} with monotonicity of $\sqrt{\cdot}$ closes it.
\end{proof}

At exactly the budget where the model retains $98.5\%$ of its accuracy, at least
$35\%$ of the attention mass is discarded.

\subsection{The converse fails: effective support does not control the knee}

\begin{definition}[Spike family]
For $n\ge0$ let $\sigma^{(n)}$ be the row on $n+2$ positions with
$\sigma^{(n)}_0 = \tfrac12$ and $\sigma^{(n)}_i = \tfrac{1}{2(n+1)}$ for
$i\ne0$. It is a probability vector.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:spikeneff}
$C(\sigma^{(n)}) = \dfrac{n+2}{4(n+1)}$, hence
$\Neff(\sigma^{(n)}) = \dfrac{4(n+1)}{n+2}\to4$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$C = (1/2)^2 + (n+1)\big(\tfrac{1}{2(n+1)}\big)^2 = \tfrac14+\tfrac{1}{4(n+1)}$;
combine and invert.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:spikemass}
For every $T$ with $|T|\le k$,
$\sum_{i\in T}\sigma^{(n)}_i \le \tfrac12 + \tfrac{k}{2(n+1)}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Dominate $\sigma^{(n)}_i$ pointwise by
$\tfrac12\mathbf{1}[i=0] + \tfrac{1}{2(n+1)}$ and sum over $T$: the indicator
contributes at most $\tfrac12$, the constant at most $k/(2(n+1))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No reverse inequality]\label{thm:noreverse}
For every fixed budget $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an
attention row $p$ with $|\Neff(p) - 4| < \varepsilon$ and
$\sum_{i\in T}p_i < \tfrac12+\varepsilon$ for every $T$ with $|T|\le k$.
Consequently no inequality of the form ``top-$k$ mass $\ge F(k,\Neff)$'' with
$F(k,4) > \tfrac12$ can hold.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:spikeneff} the first condition holds for all large $n$; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:spikemass} the second holds as soon as $k/(2(n+1)) < \varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sharp}
$\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{(\sigma^{(n)}_0)^2}{1\cdot C(\sigma^{(n)})} = 1$, so the
constant in Theorem~\ref{thm:cs} at $k=1$ cannot be improved.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The ratio equals $\big(1+\tfrac{1}{n+1}\big)^{-1}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:spikeneff}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
A row can look, by the effective-support statistic, like it uses four positions,
while hiding half its mass from every fixed budget. Concentration is a necessary
but far from sufficient handle on truncation.
\end{remark}

\section{A mechanism, and why it is forced}

\subsection{The depth leg: additive error accumulation}

Write $\Phi_d = f_{d-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_0$ for the composite of the first $d$
exact layers on a pseudometric space $X$ of hidden states, and $\Psi_d$ for the
composite of the truncated layers $g_i$.

\begin{theorem}[Depth leg]\label{thm:depth}
Suppose each $f_i$ is nonexpansive ($1$-Lipschitz) and
$\dist(g_i(x),f_i(x)) \le \varepsilon_i$ for all $x$. Then for every $x$,
\[
  \dist\big(\Psi_d(x),\Phi_d(x)\big) \;\le\; \sum_{i<d}\varepsilon_i,
\]
and with $\varepsilon_i\equiv\varepsilon$ the bound is $d\cdot\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $d$. At the step insert $f_n(\Psi_n(x))$ and apply the triangle
inequality: the first leg is $\le\varepsilon_n$, the second is
$\dist(f_n(\Psi_n x), f_n(\Phi_n x)) \le \dist(\Psi_n x, \Phi_n x)$ by
nonexpansiveness, bounded by the inductive hypothesis.
\end{proof}

Errors \emph{add}: an end-to-end budget $\delta$ imposes a per-layer budget
$\delta/d$, and the top-$k$ demand grows linearly in depth.

\subsection{The context leg: a scale-free tail}

\begin{definition}[Zipf tail]
The mass left outside the top $k$ of a row of length $\ctx$ is modelled as
$\tailA(k) = A\cdot\ctx/k$, i.e.\ a function of the fraction $x = k/\ctx$ alone,
with the $1/x$ profile and amplitude $A>0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Feasibility]\label{thm:feas}
For $\delta>0$, $d\ge1$, $k\ge1$:
$\;d\cdot\tailA(k)\le\delta \iff k \ge A\,d\,\ctx/\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The same inequality after clearing the positive denominators $k$ and $\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Least sufficient budget]\label{thm:least}
For $A,\ctx,\delta>0$ and $d\ge1$, the set
$\{k\ge1 : d\cdot\tailA(k)\le\delta\}$ has least element
$\big\lceil A\,d\,\ctx/\delta\big\rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$q = A d\,\ctx/\delta > 0$, so $\lceil q\rceil\ge1$; it is feasible because
$\lceil q\rceil\ge q$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:feas}; any feasible integer $k$
satisfies $k\ge q$, hence $k\ge\lceil q\rceil$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The attention-cost law]\label{thm:law}
Calibrate the single dimensionless constant $A/\delta = 1/32$. Then on any cell
with $d,\ctx\ge1$ and $32 \mid d\cdot\ctx$, the least sufficient budget is
exactly $k^\ast = d\cdot\ctx/32$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$A d\,\ctx/\delta = (A/\delta)(d\,\ctx) = d\,\ctx/32$, a positive integer under
the divisibility hypothesis; the ceiling of an integer is itself, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:least} applies.
\end{proof}

This reproduces $16, 32, 64$ at $d = 4, 8, 16$ with $\ctx = 128$, and $64$ at
$d = 4$, $\ctx = 512$.

\begin{theorem}[Context-invariant speedup]\label{thm:speedup}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:law}, $\ctx/k^\ast = 32/d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $d\cdot\ctx = 32m$; then $k^\ast = m$ and
$\ctx/m = 32\,\ctx/(d\,\ctx) = 32/d$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Rigidity I: the functional form is forced}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of the cost law]\label{thm:unique}
Let $K:\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\times\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\to(0,\infty)$ and
$S:\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
\begin{enumerate}
\item (depth-only speedup) $\ctx/K(d,\ctx) = S(d)$ for all $d,\ctx\ge1$;
\item (linear depth leg at unit context) $K(d,1) = d\cdot K(1,1)$ for all
      $d\ge1$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $K(d,\ctx) = d\cdot\ctx\cdot K(1,1)$ for all $d,\ctx\ge1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Evaluating (1) at $\ctx=1$ gives $1/K(d,1) = S(d)$; equating with the general
case gives $K(d,\ctx) = \ctx\cdot K(d,1)$. Substitute (2).
\end{proof}

So the bilinear form $k^\ast\propto d\cdot\ctx$ is \emph{implied} by the two
qualitative findings; the only empirical content is $K(1,1) = 1/32$.

\subsection{Rigidity II: the tail profile is forced}

\begin{theorem}[The Zipf profile is the unique depth-linear scale-free tail]
\label{thm:zipfforced}
Let $t:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous and model the per-layer tail at
fraction $x$ by $t(x)$. Fix $\delta>0$, $x_1>0$, and suppose for every $d\ge1$
the set $\{x>0 : d\,t(x)\le\delta\}$ has least element $d\,x_1$. Then
\[
  t(d\,x_1) \;=\; \frac{\delta\,x_1}{d\,x_1}\qquad\text{for every }d\ge1,
\]
i.e.\ $t(u) = \delta x_1/u$ on the measured points.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $c = d\,x_1 > 0$. Membership gives $d\,t(c)\le\delta$. Strictness would,
by continuity of $x\mapsto d\,t(x)$ at $c$, give a neighbourhood on which
$d\,t(x)<\delta$ and $x>0$; a point $x<c$ there contradicts minimality of $c$.
Hence $d\,t(c) = \delta$, so $t(c) = \delta/d = \delta x_1/c$.
\end{proof}

Every scale-free profile yields a context-invariant speedup, so
context-invariance carries no information about $t$; it is the \emph{depth} leg
that pins the shape. Combined with Theorem~\ref{thm:unique}, the empirical grid
determines the mechanism up to the single constant $1/32$.

\subsection{Capstone: an end-to-end guarantee at the law's budget}

\begin{theorem}[Truncation at $d\,\ctx/32$ is end-to-end safe]\label{thm:capstone}
Let $A,\delta>0$ with $A/\delta = 1/32$, let $32\mid d\cdot\ctx$, let each exact
layer $f_i$ be nonexpansive, and suppose
$\dist(g_i(x),f_i(x))\le\tailA(d\,\ctx/32)$ for all $i,x$. Then for every $x$,
$\dist(\Psi_d(x),\Phi_d(x))\le\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:law} says $k = d\,\ctx/32$ is feasible, i.e.\
$d\cdot\tailA(k)\le\delta$; Theorem~\ref{thm:depth} (uniform version) bounds the
end-to-end deviation by $d\cdot\tailA(k)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Why accuracy is cheaper than mass: the read-out analysis}

Let $V$ be a normed space of value vectors. The exact read-out is
$\Out(p) = \sum_{i\in s}p_i v_i$; the truncated read-out on $T$ is
$\Out_T(p) = \big(\sum_{i\in T}p_i\big)^{-1}\sum_{i\in T}p_i v_i$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:wsum}
If $p\ge0$ and $\|v_i\|\le B$ on $U$, then
$\big\|\sum_{i\in U}p_i v_i\big\| \le \big(\sum_{i\in U}p_i\big)B$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Triangle inequality, then $\|p_i v_i\| = p_i\|v_i\| \le p_i B$ termwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Truncation read-out error]\label{thm:readout}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $\sum_{i\in s}p_i = 1$, let $T\subseteq s$ with
$\rho := \sum_{i\in T}p_i > 0$, and $\|v_i\|\le B$ on $s$. Then
\[
  \big\|\Out_T(p) - \Out(p)\big\| \;\le\; 2(1-\rho)B .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Split $\Out(p) = S_R + S_T$ with $S_T = \sum_T p_iv_i$,
$S_R = \sum_{s\setminus T}p_iv_i$, tail mass $1-\rho$. Algebra gives
$\Out_T(p)-\Out(p) = (\rho^{-1}-1)S_T - S_R$. Lemma~\ref{lem:wsum} bounds
$\|S_T\|\le\rho B$ and $\|S_R\|\le(1-\rho)B$, and
$(\rho^{-1}-1)\rho B = (1-\rho)B$. The two contributions---renormalization
inflation and dropped tail---each cost $(1-\rho)B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Arg-max stability]\label{lem:argmax}
Let $f,g$ be score functions with $|g_j - f_j|\le e$ for all $j$. If
$f_j + 2e < f_c$ for all $j\ne c$, then $g_j < g_c$ for all $j\ne c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$g_j \le f_j + e < f_c - e \le g_c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Top-$k$ truncation preserves the prediction]\label{thm:preserve}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:readout}, let the score map be $L$-Lipschitz
per class, $|\score(y,j)-\score(y',j)|\le L\|y-y'\|$. If
$\score(\Out(p),j) + 4L(1-\rho)B < \score(\Out(p),c)$ for all $j\ne c$, then the
truncated model also predicts $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:readout} the score perturbation is at most
$e = L\cdot2(1-\rho)B$; the hypothesis says the exact margin exceeds $2e$; apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:argmax}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Retention threshold]\label{thm:threshold}
With logit margin $m$ (i.e.\ $\score(\Out(p),j)+m\le\score(\Out(p),c)$ for
$j\ne c$) and $L,B>0$, the prediction is preserved whenever
\[
  \rho \;>\; 1 - \frac{m}{4LB}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The hypothesis rearranges to $4L(1-\rho)B < m$, which feeds
Theorem~\ref{thm:preserve}.
\end{proof}

The threshold governing \emph{accuracy} is not the $0.98$ mass level; it is
$1 - m/(4LB)$, set by the held-out logit margin and the read-out constant. For a
healthy margin this sits far below $0.98$---precisely why the measured accuracy
knee $64$ can undercut the certified mass knee $\ge146$.

\subsection{The margin law}

\begin{definition}[Margin knee]
$k_m(A,\ctx,L,B,m) = \big\lceil 4LBA\,\ctx/m\big\rceil$: the least budget whose
scale-free tail fits inside the threshold $m/(4LB)$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:threshold}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Margin knee is least]\label{thm:mkleast}
For $A,\ctx,L,B,m>0$, $k_m$ is the least element of
$\{k\ge1 : \tailA(k)\le m/(4LB)\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:least} with $d=1$ and $\delta = m/(4LB)$, after simplifying
$A\cdot1\cdot\ctx/(m/(4LB)) = 4LBA\,\ctx/m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided margin law]\label{thm:marginlaw}
Write $x = 4LBA\,\ctx/m$ and assume $x\ge1$ (the margin channel bites). Then
\[
  \frac{m}{8LB}\;\le\;\tailA(k_m)\;\le\;\frac{m}{4LB},
\]
i.e.\ $1-\rho(k^\ast) = \Theta\!\big(m/(LB)\big)$ with explicit constants $1/8$
and $1/4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The upper bound is feasibility (Theorem~\ref{thm:mkleast}). For the lower bound,
$k_m = \lceil x\rceil < x+1 \le 2x$ because $x\ge1$; as $\tailA$ decreases in
$k$, $\tailA(k_m) \ge A\,\ctx/(2x) = m/(8LB)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Knee window]\label{thm:window}
Under the same hypotheses,
$1 \le k_m\,m/(4LBA\,\ctx) \le 2$: the dimensionless knee is confined to a
window fixed in advance, with no free constant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$x\le\lceil x\rceil\le2x$; divide by $x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity and scaling]\label{thm:mono}
$k_m$ is antitone in $m$: if $m\le m'$ then $k_{m'}\le k_m$. And the
pre-rounding budget scales exactly like $1/m$: replacing $m$ by $c\,m$ ($c>0$)
multiplies $4LBA\,\ctx/m$ by $1/c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Monotonicity of $t\mapsto C/t$ for $C\ge0$ and of the ceiling; the scaling is
algebra.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Margin lower bound at the long-context cell]\label{thm:marginnum}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $\Neff(p) = 152.11$, let $|T|\le64$, and suppose the
survival of the prediction at that budget is explained by
Theorem~\ref{thm:threshold}, i.e.\ $1 - m/(4LB) < \sum_{i\in T}p_i$ with
$L,B>0$. Then $m > 1.4\,LB$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling} gives $\sum_T p_i \le 0.65$, so
$1 - m/(4LB) < 0.65$, i.e.\ $m/(4LB) > 0.35$.
\end{proof}

A measured held-out logit margin below $1.4LB$ at that cell would refute the
margin-channel explanation of the knee.

\section{Depth rigidity: nonexpansiveness is load-bearing}

\begin{theorem}[Depth leg with general Lipschitz constant]\label{thm:lip}
If each $f_i$ is $\Lambda$-Lipschitz and each $g_i$ deviates pointwise by at
most $\varepsilon\ge0$, then
$\dist(\Psi_d(x),\Phi_d(x)) \le \varepsilon\sum_{i<d}\Lambda^i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The induction of Theorem~\ref{thm:depth} with the transport step costing a
factor $\Lambda$; the identity
$\sum_{i<n+1}\Lambda^i = 1+\Lambda\sum_{i<n}\Lambda^i$ closes the step.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Positive branch: near-isometry preserves linearity]
\label{thm:nearisom}
If $\Lambda = 1 + c/d$ with $c\ge0$, then
$\sum_{i<d}(1+c/d)^i \le d\,e^{c}$, hence
$\dist(\Psi_d x,\Phi_d x)\le e^{c}\,(d\,\varepsilon)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each term satisfies $(1+c/d)^i \le (1+c/d)^d \le (e^{c/d})^d = e^c$, using
$1+u\le e^u$; sum $d$ terms.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Negative branch: uniform expansion destroys linearity]
\label{thm:expansive}
Fix $x>0$ and set $\Lambda = 1+x$. Then
$\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i \ge d + x\,d(d-1)/2$, and for every constant $M$ there is a
depth $D$ with $\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i \ge M\,d$ for all $d\ge D$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Bernoulli: $(1+x)^i \ge 1+ix$; summing gives $d + x\,d(d-1)/2$ by Gauss. The
quadratic term beats $Md$ once $d-1\ge2M/x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No linear knee under uniform expansion]\label{cor:nolinear}
With a Zipf tail of amplitude $A>0$ over context $\ctx>0$ and budget $\delta>0$,
if the layers are uniformly $(1+x)$-Lipschitz with $x>0$, then for every
constant $M$ there is a depth beyond which every feasible budget satisfies
$k \ge M\,d$. In particular no law $k^\ast = C\cdot d$ can hold at large depth.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Feasibility reads $k \ge \big(\sum_{i<d}(1+x)^i\big)A\,\ctx/\delta$; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:expansive} with constant $M\delta/(A\,\ctx)$.
\end{proof}

The depth leg is a \emph{spectral} statement: measuring per-layer Jacobian norms
bounded away from $1$ would refute it without running a single top-$k$ sweep.

\section{Long context, and the random-$k$ control}

\begin{theorem}[Mass at the law's own budget]\label{thm:longctx}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ and suppose $C(p)\le 1/(\alpha\,\ctx)$ with $\alpha,\ctx>0$
(equivalently $\Neff \ge \alpha\,\ctx$). If $|T| \le d\,\ctx/32$ then
\[
  \sum_{i\in T}p_i \;\le\; \sqrt{\frac{d}{32\alpha}},
\]
a bound with no context length in it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$|T|\,C(p) \le (d\,\ctx/32)\cdot1/(\alpha\,\ctx) = d/(32\alpha)$; apply
Corollary~\ref{cor:massbound}.
\end{proof}

At $d=4$, $\alpha=1$ the bound is $\sqrt{1/8} = 0.354 < 1/2$.

\begin{theorem}[Pre-registered $\ctx = 1024$ prediction]\label{thm:ctx1024}
At $d = 4$, if $\Neff \ge \ctx = 1024$ (i.e.\ $C(p)\le1/1024$), then at the
predicted knee $k^\ast = 4\cdot1024/32 = 128$ the retained attention mass
satisfies $\sum_{i\in T}p_i \le 0.36$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:longctx} with $d=4$, $\alpha=1$, $\ctx=1024$ gives
$\sqrt{4/32} = 0.3535\ldots\le0.36$.
\end{proof}

The hypotheses are non-vacuous: the uniform row on $1024$ positions has
$C = 1/1024$ exactly, and any $128$ of its positions carry mass
$1/8 \le 0.36$. A run reporting $\ge0.98$ retained accuracy at $k = 128$
certifies a mass/accuracy separation of at least $2.7\times$; a run reporting
more than $0.36$ retained \emph{mass} refutes the linear growth of $\Neff$.

\begin{lemma}[Double counting]\label{lem:doublecount}
For a finite set $s$, a fixed $i\in s$ and $k\ge0$, the number of
$(k+1)$-subsets of $s$ containing $i$ is $\binom{|s|-1}{k}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$T\mapsto T\setminus\{i\}$ is a bijection onto the $k$-subsets of
$s\setminus\{i\}$, with inverse $U\mapsto U\cup\{i\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Total and average mass over random subsets]\label{thm:random}
For any $p:s\to\mathbb{R}$ and $k\ge0$,
\[
  \sum_{\substack{T\subseteq s\\|T| = k+1}}\ \sum_{i\in T}p_i
  \;=\; \binom{|s|-1}{k}\sum_{i\in s}p_i ,
\]
and if $k+1\le|s|$, the average mass retained by a uniformly random
$(k+1)$-subset is exactly $\frac{k+1}{|s|}\sum_{i\in s}p_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Exchange the order of summation and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:doublecount} to each
$i$. For the average, divide by $\binom{|s|}{k+1}$ and use
$\binom{|s|}{k+1}(k+1) = |s|\binom{|s|-1}{k}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Selection-gain bound]\label{thm:gain}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$, $T\subseteq s$ with $|T| = k\ge1$, and $C(p)\le1/\Neff$ with
$\Neff,\ctx>0$. Then
\[
  \frac{\sum_{i\in T}p_i}{k/\ctx} \;\le\; \frac{\ctx}{\sqrt{k\,\Neff}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Corollary~\ref{cor:massbound} gives $\sum_T p_i \le \sqrt{k/\Neff}$; the claim
follows from $\sqrt{k/\Neff}\cdot\sqrt{k\Neff} = k$ and cross-multiplication.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:gainnum}
With $\ctx = 512$, $k = 64$, $\Neff = 152.11$, the selection advantage in
retained mass is at most $5.2$, since $\sqrt{64\times152.11} > 98.6$ and
$512/98.6 < 5.2$.
\end{corollary}

Selection can buy at most $5.2\times$ the control's mass, while the measured
accuracy gaps are $+7.6$ and $+5.2$ percentage points: the control gap is a
statement about \emph{which} positions are kept, not a bulk mass effect.

\subsection{The concentration drift is not amplitude drift}

\begin{theorem}[Scale-free tail caps the effective support]\label{thm:cap}
Let $p\ge0$ on $s$ with $C(p)>0$ and $A\,\ctx>0$. If some head $T$ with
$|T|\le\lceil2A\,\ctx\rceil$ satisfies
$\sum_{i\in T}p_i \ge 1 - A\,\ctx/\lceil2A\,\ctx\rceil$, then
$\Neff(p) \le 8A\,\ctx + 4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Set $K = \lceil2A\,\ctx\rceil$. Then $A\,\ctx/K \le 1/2$, so the head mass is
$r\ge1/2$. Theorem~\ref{thm:massknee} inverted gives
$\Neff \le |T|/r^2 \le 4K$, and $K < 2A\,\ctx+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Amplitude forced by a depth-linear knee]\label{thm:amp}
If at some depth $d\ge1$ the least sufficient budget $A\,d\,\ctx/\delta$ equals
the measured $d\,\ctx/32$, then $A = \delta/32$---with no $d$ in it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Cancel the positive factor $d\,\ctx$ from both sides.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The conjectured amplitude drift is refuted]\label{cor:ampdrift}
If the depth-linear knee holds at $d=4$ and $d=16$ with the same
$\delta,\ctx$, then $A_4 = A_{16} = \delta/32$, hence
$A_{16}\cdot16 = 4(A_4\cdot4) > A_4\cdot4$. The product $A(d)\cdot d$ is not
constant; it grows linearly. The $13\%$ drift in $\Neff$ cannot be a drift of
the tail amplitude.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Depth-independent ceiling]\label{cor:ceiling}
Substituting $A = \delta/32$ into Theorem~\ref{thm:cap} gives, at every depth,
$\Neff \le \delta\,\ctx/4 + 4$. All three drifting measurements sit under one
ceiling; unbounded growth of $\Neff$ with depth would refute the scale-free
tail.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[The deepest cell bounds the error budget]\label{cor:budget}
Cell A reports $\Neff = 52.73$ at $\ctx = 128$; the ceiling reads
$\Neff \le 32\delta + 4$, whence $\delta \ge 1.52$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[The margin is depth-independent too]\label{thm:margindepth}
If the budget the margin channel asks for, $4LBA\,d\,\ctx/m$, equals the
measured $d\,\ctx/32$ at some depth, then $m = 128\,LBA$---again with no $d$ in
it. Hence the margins at $d=4$ and $d=16$ (same context) must be \emph{equal},
not inversely proportional to depth; a measured ratio $m(16)/m(4)\approx1/4$
would refute the mechanism.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Cancel $d\,\ctx\ne0$ from $4LBA\,d\,\ctx = (d\,\ctx/32)\,m$.
\end{proof}

\section{Stability of the measured knee, and grid completion}

\begin{theorem}[Knee stability]\label{thm:stab}
Let $\mathcal{K}$ be the swept budget set, $R$ the measured retained-accuracy
curve, $\theta$ the threshold, $\eta\ge0$ a perturbation level, $k\in\mathcal{K}$.
Suppose
\begin{enumerate}
\item $|R'(j)-R(j)|\le\eta$ for all $j$;
\item $R(k)\ge\theta+\eta$;
\item $R(j)+\eta<\theta$ for every $j\in\mathcal{K}$ with $j<k$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $k$ is the least element of $\{j\in\mathcal{K} : R'(j)\ge\theta\}$: the
rerun reports the same knee.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Membership: $R'(k)\ge R(k)-\eta\ge\theta$. Minimality: if some $j<k$ in
$\mathcal{K}$ had $R'(j)\ge\theta$, then $R(j)\ge R'(j)-\eta\ge\theta-\eta$,
contradicting (3).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cell A is seed-robust up to $\eta = 0.005$]\label{cor:stabA}
With $R(8)=0.858$, $R(16)=0.922$, $R(32)=0.970$, $R(64)=0.996$, $R(96)=0.999$,
$R(128)=1.000$ and $\theta = 0.98$: any rerun within $0.005$ reports
$k^\ast = 64 = 16\cdot128/32$. Indeed $R(64) = 0.996 \ge 0.985$ and
$R(32)+0.005 = 0.975 < 0.98$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Cell B is seed-robust up to $\eta = 0.003$]\label{cor:stabB}
With $R(16)=0.965$, $R(32)=0.976$, $R(64)=0.985$, $R(128)=0.993$,
$R(256)=0.998$, $R(384)=1.000$: any rerun within $0.003$ reports
$k^\ast = 64 = 4\cdot512/32$. Indeed $R(64) = 0.985\ge0.983$ and
$R(32)+0.003 = 0.979 < 0.98$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Grid completion]\label{thm:gridcomplete}
The observed seed-to-seed spread is $\pm0.002$, strictly inside both tolerance
windows. Hence any rerun of either corner cell within the observed spread
reports exactly the predicted knee: $16\cdot128/32 = 64$ at cell A and
$4\cdot512/32 = 64$ at cell B.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$0.002\le0.005$ and $0.002\le0.003$; apply Corollaries~\ref{cor:stabA} and
\ref{cor:stabB}.
\end{proof}

No seed could have moved either knee. Combined with the earlier cells, every
measured cell of the depth-by-context grid is confirmed at two independent
seeds, with every knee landing exactly on $d\cdot\ctx/32$. A previously
suspected erosion of the long-context pass margin ($0.003$ at one seed) does not
reproduce ($0.005$ at the next): the margin fluctuates by $\pm0.002$ rather than
trending.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Knee sweep.} Given a model, a held-out set and a budget ladder
$\mathcal{K}$: (i) evaluate full-attention accuracy $a_{\mathrm{full}}$; (ii) for
each $k\in\mathcal{K}$ in increasing order, evaluate top-$k$-truncated accuracy
$a_k$ and set $R(k) = a_k/a_{\mathrm{full}}$; (iii) return the first $k$ with
$R(k)\ge0.98$. Cost: $|\mathcal{K}|+1$ held-out passes. The truncation is
data-free---it depends only on each row's own weights---so there is no leakage
from held-out labels.

\paragraph{Certified mass ceiling.} Given $\Neff$ and $k$, return
$\min\{1,\sqrt{k/\Neff}\}$: by Corollary~\ref{cor:massbound} a valid upper bound
on the mass any $k$ positions can carry, computable in $O(1)$ from a statistic
costing one pass over the row. Its companion $\rho^2\Neff$ lower-bounds the
budget needed to retain mass $\rho$.

\paragraph{Knee-stability certificate.} Given a measured curve $R$ on
$\mathcal{K}$, a threshold $\theta$ and the reported knee $k$: compute the pass
margin $R(k)-\theta$ and the fail margin $\min_{j<k}(\theta - R(j))$; the
certified tolerance is the minimum of the two. Any rerun within that tolerance
reports the same knee by Theorem~\ref{thm:stab}. Cost: $O(|\mathcal{K}|)$.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What is and is not explained}

The central negative result is that attention concentration does not explain
top-$k$ truncation, and two theorems make it precise in opposite directions.
Theorem~\ref{thm:sep} says the measured effective support makes mass retention
\emph{too expensive} to be the mechanism. Theorem~\ref{thm:noreverse} says no
repair is available in the other direction: rows with $\Neff$ arbitrarily close
to $4$ can hide half their mass from every fixed budget.

What \emph{is} explained: the law follows from additive error accumulation
across nonexpansive layers plus a scale-free tail
(Theorems~\ref{thm:depth}, \ref{thm:feas}, \ref{thm:law}); the mechanism is
forced by the grid's own qualitative content
(Theorems~\ref{thm:unique}, \ref{thm:zipfforced}); the mass--accuracy gap is
exactly the slack the decision margin provides
(Theorems~\ref{thm:readout}--\ref{thm:threshold}); and its size is pinned
two-sidedly (Theorem~\ref{thm:marginlaw}).

\subsection{Scope and limitations}

The empirical grid is small-scale: model dimension $64$, four heads, $2000$
training steps, a $4097$-token vocabulary, five novels. Absolute accuracies
($0.157$--$0.162$) are those of a small word-level language model. What
transfers is structural---the \emph{shape} of the law, the certified separation,
the rigidity theorems---not the specific constant $1/32$, a calibration of one
dimensionless ratio $A/\delta$ at this scale.

The theorems of Sections 2--7 are unconditional statements about weight vectors,
Lipschitz stacks and threshold crossings. Where measured numbers enter
(Theorems~\ref{thm:sep}, \ref{thm:ceiling}, \ref{thm:marginnum},
Corollaries~\ref{cor:gainnum}, \ref{cor:budget}, \ref{cor:stabA},
\ref{cor:stabB}), they appear as explicit numerical hypotheses.

Two hypotheses deserve scrutiny. \emph{Nonexpansiveness} is not verified
directly; Section 5 turns it into a falsifiable spectral test and shows the
conclusion survives $\Lambda\le1+c/d$ but not a fixed $\Lambda>1$. \emph{The
Zipf tail} is not verified directly either, but
Theorem~\ref{thm:zipfforced} shows it is the unique scale-free profile
compatible with the measured depth-linear knee.

\subsection{Practical reading}

At depth $d$ and any context length, restricting each attention row to its top
$\ctx\cdot d/32$ positions retains $\ge98\%$ of held-out accuracy, a speedup of
$32/d$. The speedup is context-invariant, so the lever does not degrade as
windows grow, and it is seed-independent at every measured corner: no
per-instance re-measurement is needed inside the measured grid. Shallow models
get the biggest win ($8\times$ at $d=4$).

Two implementation notes follow. Selection matters: the random-$k$ control at
the same budget loses $5$--$10$ accuracy points, and by
Corollary~\ref{cor:gainnum} at most a factor $5.2$ of that can be a bulk-mass
effect. And mass is the wrong monitoring statistic: by
Theorem~\ref{thm:ceiling} a healthy deployment will be discarding a third or
more of its attention mass.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{Immediate experiments.} (i) $\ctx = 1024$ at $d = 4$:
Theorem~\ref{thm:ctx1024} pre-registers a mass ceiling of $0.36$ at the
predicted knee $k^\ast = 128$; a run reporting $\ge0.98$ retained accuracy there
certifies a $2.7\times$ mass/accuracy separation, and one reporting more than
$0.36$ mass refutes the linear growth of $\Neff$. (ii) $\ctx = 512$ at
$d = 8, 16$, and the remaining $d = 8$, $\ctx = 256$ corner. (iii) Log the
held-out logit margin: Theorem~\ref{thm:marginnum} predicts $m > 1.4LB$ at the
long-context cell, and Theorem~\ref{thm:margindepth} predicts the margin is
depth-independent, so measuring $m$ at $d = 4$ and $d = 16$ is a direct two-point
test. (iv) Measure per-layer Jacobian norms: by Theorem~\ref{thm:nearisom}
versus Corollary~\ref{cor:nolinear}, a spectral norm bounded away from $1$
refutes the depth leg with no sweep at all.

\paragraph{Theory.} Strengthen the margin law from the interval
$[m/(8LB), m/(4LB)]$ to an asymptotic constant; the factor-two window is an
artifact of the ceiling in the knee definition. Extend the read-out analysis
from a single attention layer to interaction between heads. Test both
structural hypotheses directly: the tail profile by measuring
$\mathrm{tail}(k)$ at several $k$, nonexpansiveness spectrally.

\paragraph{Sharper questions raised by the rigidity results.} The tail amplitude
is forced to be $A = \delta/32$ at every depth
(Theorem~\ref{thm:amp}), which pushes the observed $13\%$ drift of $\Neff$ with
depth onto some other channel: what is it? The depth-independent ceiling
$\Neff \le \delta\,\ctx/4 + 4$ must contain the drift, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:budget} shows the deepest cell already forces
$\delta \ge 1.52$. Measuring $\Neff$ at $d = 32$ would either continue the drift
toward the ceiling or break it.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

THRESHOLD: float = 0.98


def retained_accuracy_curve(
    full_accuracy: float,
    truncated_accuracy: Callable[[int], float],
    budgets: Sequence[int],
) -> Dict[int, float]:
    """Evaluate R(k) = accuracy(top-k) / accuracy(full) on a budget ladder.

    `truncated_accuracy(k)` is one held-out evaluation pass with every attention
    row restricted to its k largest weights and renormalised. The truncation is
    data-free: it reads only the row's own weights, so no held-out label
    information can leak into the choice of retained positions.
    """
    if full_accuracy <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("full-attention accuracy must be positive")
    return {k: truncated_accuracy(k) / full_accuracy for k in sorted(budgets)}


def knee(curve: Dict[int, float], threshold: float = THRESHOLD) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest swept budget whose retained accuracy reaches the threshold."""
    for k in sorted(curve):
        if curve[k] >= threshold:
            return k
    return None


def stability_certificate(
    curve: Dict[int, float],
    k_star: int,
    threshold: float = THRESHOLD,
) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Return (pass margin, fail margin, certified tolerance eta).

    Any rerun of the same sweep whose retained accuracies all stay within the
    certified tolerance of `curve` is guaranteed to report the same knee: it
    still clears the threshold at k_star, and it still fails at every smaller
    swept budget.
    """
    pass_margin = curve[k_star] - threshold
    smaller: List[float] = [threshold - curve[j] for j in curve if j < k_star]
    fail_margin = min(smaller) if smaller else float("inf")
    return pass_margin, fail_margin, min(pass_margin, fail_margin)


def knee_with_certificate(
    full_accuracy: float,
    truncated_accuracy: Callable[[int], float],
    budgets: Sequence[int],
    threshold: float = THRESHOLD,
) -> Tuple[Optional[int], float]:
    """Full pipeline: sweep, locate the knee, certify its seed-stability."""
    curve = retained_accuracy_curve(full_accuracy, truncated_accuracy, budgets)
    k_star = knee(curve, threshold)
    if k_star is None:
        return None, 0.0
    return k_star, stability_certificate(curve, k_star, threshold)[2]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Sequence, Tuple


def collision_mass(row: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Collision mass sum_i p_i^2 of an attention row."""
    return sum(x * x for x in row)


def effective_support(row: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """N_eff = 1 / sum_i p_i^2, the inverse participation ratio."""
    c = collision_mass(row)
    if c <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("collision mass must be positive")
    return 1.0 / c


def mass_ceiling(k: int, n_eff: float) -> float:
    """Largest mass ANY k positions of a row with this N_eff can carry.

    Cauchy-Schwarz gives (sum_{i in T} p_i)^2 <= |T| * sum_i p_i^2, hence the
    ceiling sqrt(k / N_eff). It holds for arbitrary index sets, so in particular
    for the top-k set; no sortedness, positivity or normalisation is used.
    """
    if k < 0 or n_eff <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("k must be nonnegative and N_eff positive")
    return min(1.0, math.sqrt(k / n_eff))


def mass_knee_floor(rho: float, n_eff: float) -> int:
    """Fewest positions that could possibly retain a fraction rho of the mass.

    The same inequality read backwards: |T| >= rho^2 * N_eff.
    """
    if not 0.0 <= rho <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("rho must lie in [0, 1]")
    return math.ceil(rho * rho * n_eff)


def separation_report(n_eff: float, accuracy_knee: int,
                      retained_accuracy: float,
                      rho: float = 0.98) -> Tuple[int, float, float]:
    """Quantify the gap between the mass knee and the measured accuracy knee.

    Returns (mass-knee floor, mass ceiling at the accuracy knee, separation
    factor). A separation factor above 1 means the measured accuracy knee is
    strictly cheaper than any budget that could retain the mass, so mass
    retention cannot be the mechanism behind the measured truncation tolerance.
    """
    floor = mass_knee_floor(rho, n_eff)
    ceiling = mass_ceiling(accuracy_knee, n_eff)
    return floor, ceiling, retained_accuracy / ceiling


def long_context_mass_bound(depth: int, alpha: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """Context-independent mass ceiling at the law's own budget d*ctx/32.

    If the effective support keeps pace with context, N_eff >= alpha * ctx, then
    at k = d*ctx/32 the retained mass is at most sqrt(d / (32 alpha)) -- a bound
    with no context length in it.
    """
    return math.sqrt(depth / (32.0 * alpha))

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def geometric_factor(lipschitz: float, depth: int) -> float:
    """Error-amplification factor sum_{i<d} Lambda^i of a d-layer stack.

    Lambda = 1 (nonexpansive layers) gives exactly d: truncation errors ADD
    along depth. Lambda = 1 + c/d (near-isometry) stays within exp(c) of d. A
    fixed Lambda > 1 makes the factor grow superlinearly, which is incompatible
    with a knee linear in depth.
    """
    if lipschitz == 1.0:
        return float(depth)
    return (lipschitz ** depth - 1.0) / (lipschitz - 1.0)


def zipf_tail(amplitude: float, ctx: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Scale-free tail A * ctx / k left outside the top k of a length-ctx row."""
    if k <= 0:
        raise ValueError("budget must be positive")
    return amplitude * ctx / k


def least_sufficient_budget(amplitude: float, error_budget: float,
                            depth: int, ctx: int,
                            lipschitz: float = 1.0) -> int:
    """Smallest k whose accumulated truncation error fits the end-to-end budget.

    Feasibility reads  G(Lambda, d) * A * ctx / k <= delta, so the least
    admissible integer budget is ceil(G * A * ctx / delta). At Lambda = 1 this
    is ceil(A * d * ctx / delta), which with the calibrated ratio
    A / delta = 1/32 is exactly d * ctx / 32.
    """
    if amplitude <= 0.0 or error_budget <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("amplitude and error budget must be positive")
    factor = geometric_factor(lipschitz, depth)
    return math.ceil(factor * amplitude * ctx / error_budget)


def cost_law_budget(depth: int, ctx: int) -> int:
    """The calibrated law k* = d * ctx / 32."""
    if (depth * ctx) % 32 != 0:
        raise ValueError("32 must divide d * ctx")
    return depth * ctx // 32


def speedup(depth: int, ctx: int) -> float:
    """Attention speedup ctx / k* = 32 / d -- independent of context length."""
    return ctx / cost_law_budget(depth, ctx)


def margin_knee(amplitude: float, ctx: int, lipschitz_readout: float,
                value_bound: float, margin: float) -> int:
    """Budget selected by the margin channel: ceil(4 L B A ctx / m).

    A prediction survives any score perturbation below half its margin; a
    renormalised top-k truncation moves the read-out by at most 2(1-rho)B, and
    an L-Lipschitz score map turns that into 2L(1-rho)B. The prediction is
    therefore safe once 4 L (1-rho) B < m, i.e. once the tail fits inside
    m / (4 L B).
    """
    return math.ceil(4.0 * lipschitz_readout * value_bound
                     * amplitude * ctx / margin)


def margin_law_window(amplitude: float, ctx: int, lipschitz_readout: float,
                      value_bound: float, margin: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Return (lower bound, actual deficit, upper bound) of the margin law.

    The attention deficit at the margin knee is squeezed between m/(8LB) and
    m/(4LB): it is Theta(m / (L B)), governed by the logit margin and the
    read-out constant alone, and not by any fixed mass level.
    """
    k_m = margin_knee(amplitude, ctx, lipschitz_readout, value_bound, margin)
    deficit = zipf_tail(amplitude, ctx, k_m)
    lo = margin / (8.0 * lipschitz_readout * value_bound)
    hi = margin / (4.0 * lipschitz_readout * value_bound)
    return lo, deficit, hi


def grid_table(cells: List[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Dict[Tuple[int, int], Tuple[int, float]]:

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from itertools import combinations
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def exact_mean_random_mass(row: Sequence[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Mean mass of a uniformly random k-subset, by exhaustive enumeration.

    Exponential in the row length; used only to confirm the closed form on small
    rows. Every position lies in exactly C(n-1, k-1) of the k-subsets, so the
    total mass over all subsets is C(n-1, k-1) * (total mass) and the mean is
    (k/n) * (total mass).
    """
    n = len(row)
    if not 0 <= k <= n:
        raise ValueError("k must lie between 0 and the row length")
    subsets = list(combinations(range(n), k))
    return sum(sum(row[i] for i in S) for S in subsets) / len(subsets)


def closed_form_random_mass(row: Sequence[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Closed form: a random k-subset retains (k/n) of the mass, exactly."""
    n = len(row)
    return (k / n) * sum(row)


def sampled_random_mass(row: Sequence[float], k: int, trials: int = 20000,
                        seed: int = 12345) -> float:
    """Monte-Carlo estimate of the control's mean mass, matching the harness."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(row)
    idx = list(range(n))
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        total += sum(row[i] for i in rng.sample(idx, k))
    return total / trials


def selection_gain_ceiling(ctx: int, k: int, n_eff: float) -> float:
    """Upper bound on how much more MASS selection can buy than the control.

    Selection retains at most sqrt(k / N_eff); the control retains k / ctx on
    average; the ratio is at most ctx / sqrt(k * N_eff). The bound shrinks as
    the effective support approaches the context length, so any accuracy gap
    that exceeds what this factor can explain is a statement about WHICH
    positions are kept, not about bulk mass.
    """
    return ctx / math.sqrt(k * n_eff)


def control_report(row: Sequence[float], k: int, ctx: int,
                   n_eff: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    """(selected mass, control mean mass, observed ratio, certified ceiling)."""
    selected = sum(sorted(row, reverse=True)[:k])
    control = closed_form_random_mass(row, k)
    return selected, control, selected / control, selection_gain_ceiling(ctx, k, n_eff)

from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def spike_row(n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Spike-plus-uniform probability row on n+2 positions."""
    row = np.full(n + 2, 0.5 / (n + 1))
    row[0] = 0.5
    return row


def effective_support(p: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """N_eff = 1 / sum_i p_i^2."""
    return float(1.0 / np.sum(p ** 2))


def topk_mass(p: np.ndarray, k: int) -> float:
    """Mass of the k largest entries."""
    return float(np.sort(p)[::-1][:k].sum())


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax_a, ax_b, ax_c) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16.0, 4.8))

          <span><span class="sw" style="background:var(--deep);height:0;border-top:2px dashed var(--deep)"></span>the law's budget k* = d·ctx/32</span>
          <span><span class="sw" style="background:var(--warn);height:0;border-top:2px dashed var(--warn)"></span>cheapest possible 98 %-mass budget</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="readouts">
      <div class="ro"><div class="k">Law's budget k*</div><div class="v" id="ks">64</div>
        <div class="n">d · ctx / 32</div></div>
      <div class="ro"><div class="k">Speedup</div><div class="v" id="sp">8.0×</div>
        <div class="n">ctx / k* = 32 / d, context-invariant</div></div>
      <div class="ro"><div class="k">Mass ceiling at k*</div><div class="v" id="mc">0.649</div>
        <div class="n">√(k*/N<sub>eff</sub>): no k* positions can carry more</div></div>
      <div class="ro"><div class="k">98 %-mass budget</div><div class="v" id="mk">147</div>
        <div class="n">≥ 0.98<sup>2</sup> · N<sub>eff</sub> positions</div></div>

        <div class="n">accuracy retained ÷ mass retainable</div></div>
      <div class="ro"><div class="k">Selection ceiling</div><div class="v" id="sg">5.19×</div>
        <div class="n">most extra mass selection can buy over a random-k control</div></div>
    </div>

    <details>
      <summary>Where the mass ceiling comes from (Cauchy–Schwarz, one line)</summary>
      <p>For <em>any</em> set T of retained positions,
      (Σ<sub>i∈T</sub> p<sub>i</sub>)<sup>2</sup> ≤ |T| ·
      Σ<sub>i∈T</sub> p<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> ≤ |T| ·
      Σ<sub>i</sub> p<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> = |T| / N<sub>eff</sub>.
      Taking square roots, the mass any k positions can carry is at most
      √(k / N<sub>eff</sub>). No hypothesis is used — not sortedness, not that T is
      the top-k set, not even positivity for the squared form. Read backwards, retaining
      a fraction ρ of the mass costs at least ρ<sup>2</sup> N<sub>eff</sub>
      positions. At the measured N<sub>eff</sub> = 152.11 that is more than 146 positions
      for ρ = 0.98, against a measured accuracy knee of 64.</p>
    </details>

    <details>
      <summary>Why accuracy survives a mass loss this large</summary>
      <p>Truncating a row to mass ρ and renormalising moves the layer's output vector
      by at most 2(1−ρ)B, where B bounds the value vectors — one factor
      (1−ρ)B for the dropped tail, one for the renormalisation inflation. A
      prediction is an arg-max, and an arg-max survives any perturbation below half its
      margin over the runner-up. With an L-Lipschitz read-out, the prediction is therefore
      safe as soon as 4L(1−ρ)B < m, i.e. as soon as
      <code>ρ > 1 − m/(4LB)</code>. The threshold that governs
      <i>accuracy</i> is set by the logit margin m, not by any fixed mass level. And the
      deficit at the resulting knee is pinned two-sidedly:
      m/(8LB) ≤ 1−ρ(k*) ≤ m/(4LB).</p>
    </details>

    <details>
      <summary>Why the budget must be proportional to d · ctx</summary>
      <p>Two qualitative facts pin the whole functional form. If the speedup
      ctx/K(d,ctx) depends only on the depth, and the budget at unit context is linear in
      depth, K(d,1) = d·K(1,1), then evaluating the first fact at ctx = 1 gives
      K(d,ctx) = ctx·K(d,1) = d·ctx·K(1,1). Only the single constant
      K(1,1) = 1/32 is fitted. Moreover, among scale-free tail profiles t(k/ctx), the
      1/x shape is the <i>unique</i> one compatible with a depth-linear knee: at the least
      feasible fraction the constraint must be tight, so d·t(d x<sub>1</sub>) =
      δ, giving t(u) = δx<sub>1</sub>/u.</p>
    </details>

(function(){

  const SWEEP_B = {16:0.965,32:0.976,64:0.985,128:0.993,256:0.998,384:1.000};

    const neff= +el('n').value;
    const acc = +el('a').value;
    const kstar = Math.max(1, Math.round(d*ctx/32));

  const ceiling = (k,neff) => Math.min(1, Math.sqrt(k/neff));

  function draw(s){
    const W = cv.width, H = cv.height;
    const L = 78, R = 26, T = 28, B = 58;
    const pw = W-L-R, ph = H-T-B;
    cx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    cx.fillStyle = '#fff'; cx.fillRect(0,0,W,H);

    const kmin = 1, kmax = Math.max(s.ctx, 16);
    const X = k => L + pw * (Math.log(k)-Math.log(kmin))/(Math.log(kmax)-Math.log(kmin));
    const Y = v => T + ph * (1 - v);

    // grid
    cx.strokeStyle = '#eef1f6'; cx.lineWidth = 1;

      cx.fillText(v.toFixed(1), L-9, Y(v)+4);
    }
    cx.textAlign='center';
    for(let e=0; Math.pow(2,e)<=kmax; e++){
      const k = Math.pow(2,e); if(k<kmin) continue;
      if(e%2) continue;

    cx.fillStyle='#5b6473'; cx.font='13.5px -apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif';
    cx.fillText('attention budget k  (log scale)', L+pw/2, T+ph+46);

    cx.fillStyle='#7b8494'; cx.textAlign='left';
    cx.fillText('retention threshold 0.98', L+8, Y(0.98)-7);

    cx.lineWidth=2.6; cx.beginPath();

      const y = Y(ceiling(k, s.neff));

    const sweep = (s.ctx>=256)? SWEEP_B : SWEEP_A;
    cx.strokeStyle=getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--acc').trim();
    cx.fillStyle=cx.strokeStyle; cx.lineWidth=2.6; cx.beginPath(); first=true;

      if(k>kmax) return;
      const y=Y(sweep[k]);
      if(first){cx.moveTo(X(k),y);first=false;} else cx.lineTo(X(k),y);
    });
    cx.stroke();
    Object.keys(sweep).map(Number).sort((a,b)=>a-b).forEach(k=>{
      if(k>kmax) return;
      cx.beginPath(); cx.arc(X(k),Y(sweep[k]),4.2,0,7); cx.fill();
    });

    // the law's budget
    const kx = Math.min(Math.max(s.kstar,kmin),kmax);
    cx.strokeStyle=getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--deep').trim();
    cx.setLineDash([6,4]); cx.lineWidth=2;
    cx.beginPath(); cx.moveTo(X(kx),T); cx.lineTo(X(kx),T+ph); cx.stroke();
    cx.setLineDash([]);
    cx.fillStyle=cx.strokeStyle; cx.textAlign='left';
    cx.fillText('k* = '+s.kstar, X(kx)+7, T+16);

    // the 98%-mass budget
    const mk = 0.98*0.98*s.neff;
    if(mk>=kmin && mk<=kmax){
      cx.strokeStyle=getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--warn').trim();
      cx.setLineDash([4,4]); cx.lineWidth=1.8;
      cx.beginPath(); cx.moveTo(X(mk),T); cx.lineTo(X(mk),T+ph); cx.stroke();
      cx.setLineDash([]);
      cx.fillStyle=cx.strokeStyle;
      cx.fillText('98 % mass needs '+Math.ceil(mk), X(mk)+7, T+38);
    }

    // separation arrow at k*
    const cAt = ceiling(s.kstar, s.neff);
    if(s.acc > cAt + 0.01 && kx>=kmin && kx<=kmax){
      cx.strokeStyle='#c62828'; cx.lineWidth=2.4;
      cx.beginPath(); cx.moveTo(X(kx),Y(cAt)); cx.lineTo(X(kx),Y(s.acc)); cx.stroke();
      for(const [yy,dir] of [[Y(cAt),1],[Y(s.acc),-1]]){
        cx.beginPath(); cx.moveTo(X(kx),yy);
        cx.lineTo(X(kx)-5, yy+dir*9); cx.lineTo(X(kx)+5, yy+dir*9);
        cx.closePath(); cx.fillStyle='#c62828'; cx.fill();
      }
      cx.fillStyle='#c62828'; cx.textAlign='left';
      cx.fillText('certified separation', X(kx)+9, (Y(cAt)+Y(s.acc))/2);
    }
  }

  function refresh(){
    const s = state();
    el('vd').textContent = s.d;
    el('vc').textContent = s.ctx;
    el('vn').textContent = s.neff.toFixed(1);
    el('va').textContent = s.acc.toFixed(3);

    const cAt = ceiling(s.kstar, s.neff);
    const mk  = Math.ceil(0.98*0.98*s.neff);
    const sg  = s.ctx/Math.sqrt(s.kstar*s.neff);

    el('ks').textContent = s.kstar;
    el('sp').textContent = (s.ctx/s.kstar).toFixed(1)+'\u00d7';
    el('mc').textContent = cAt.toFixed(3);
    el('mk').textContent = mk;
    el('sf').textContent = (s.acc/cAt).toFixed(2)+'\u00d7';
    el('sg').textContent = sg.toFixed(2)+'\u00d7';

    const v = el('verdict');
    if(mk > s.kstar){
      v.className = 'verdict ok';
      v.innerHTML = '<b>Certified separation.</b> Retaining 98 % of the attention '+
        '<i>mass</i> would cost at least <b>'+mk+'</b> positions, but the law\u2019s budget is only '+
        '<b>'+s.kstar+'</b>. At that budget no set of positions can carry more than <b>'+
        cAt.toFixed(3)+'</b> of the mass, yet the measured retained accuracy is <b>'+
        s.acc.toFixed(3)+'</b> \u2014 a factor <b>'+(s.acc/cAt).toFixed(2)+'</b> apart. '+
        'Mass retention cannot be the mechanism.';
    } else {
      v.className = 'verdict bad';
      v.innerHTML = '<b>No separation at this setting.</b> The law\u2019s budget <b>'+s.kstar+

        'Lower the depth, or raise the effective support, to reach the measured regime.';

    tb.appendChild(tr);

  ['d','c','n','a'].forEach(id=>el(id).addEventListener('input', refresh));
  refresh();
})();
